\begin{center}
{\Large\bfseries Acme Archipelago: a DAG for one candidate pair\par}
\vspace{0.4em}
{\normalsize Known ages, equal reproduction, and lethal sampling\par}
\end{center}
\newcommand{\Ju}{\mathrm{Ju}}
\newcommand{\Ad}{\mathrm{Ad}}


We consider two distinct, sampled females: a _candidate offspring_, denoted
by the subscript $\mathrm{Ju}$, and a _candidate mother_, denoted by subscript
$\mathrm{Ad}$. These are roles in a comparison: the candidate offspring may
be an adult when sampled, but is called the "juvenile" when being compared as
a candidate offspring. The graph represents the marginal probability
of one pair of individuals, _conditioned on their ages and sampling years_.  The CKMR pseudo-likelihood
is formed by multiplying these marginal probabilities over all pairs of individuals.
It is a pseudolikelihood because those pairs are not necessarily independent, though
in large populations under sparse sampling, this can be a good approximation.  As
discussed in the workshop, the product
over all pairs can be reduced to a product of Poisson probabilities over the
different combinations of the juvenile and adult covariates upon which the probabilities
are conditioned (in this case, age and sampling year). 

![A single-pair model for the Acme Archipelago represented as an acyclic directed graph (DAG).  See the text for explanation.](figures/acme-dag.pdf){#fig-acme width=80% fig-pos='H'}

In the DAG above, circular nodes shaded with gray fill denote observed quantities;
the unshaded circular nodes are unobserved variables. Dark pink fill denotes a parameter to be estimated. Nodes with pink outlines mark
quantities whose values (or the conditional distributions of those values) depend
on the parameter values.
These are values that must be recalculated
during separate computations of the pseudo-log-likelihood during optimization.
Dashed nodes---and dashed arrows entering them---identify
_bookkeeping intermediates_. These are values that can be deterministically
determined by the observed covariates and, hence, could be removed from the model
specification; however I find that explicitly including them provides a helpful
reminder of what they are, and representing them explicitly might become useful
later when covariates are uncertain.  Shaded gray diamonds denote fixed inputs or modeling choices.


# What each node means

We use $A$ for age at sampling and $Y$ for year of sampling.
The recorded ages and sampling years are the covariates observed on the samples:
$A_{\mathrm{Ju}}$, $Y_{\mathrm{Ju}}$, $A_{\mathrm{Ad}}$, $Y_{\mathrm{Ad}}$.
In the Acme Archipelago example, we condition on these data, on both individuals
being female, and on the comparison being included in the analysis. Since we are
conditioning on the ages and sampling years (and because they are observed without
error) we do not need to know or specify a distribution for
sampled ages and years to write down this conditional likelihood.

The rose-filled nodes show the parameters. They are $\theta=(N_{0,f},\lambda)$:
adult female abundance at the reference year and an instantaneous exponential
rate of increase, such that $N_{t,f} = N_{0,f}\exp\{\lambda (t - y_0)\}$.
The reference year $y_0$ is a modeling choice, so it is shown as a diamond node.
It is typically set to the earliest juvenvile birth year.  It is worth pointing
out here that $N_{0,f}$ counts the number of _mature_ adult females.

There are two bookkeeping intermediate nodes in the graph.  The first is $B_\Ju$,
the birth year of the juvenile.  This can be calculated simply as $B_\Ju = Y_\Ju - A_\Ju$,
but it is an extremely important quantity that warrants its own node, even if if it
is just a deterministic function of the juvenile's covariates.  The second bookkeeping
intermediate is $\mathring{A}_\Ad$. This can also be calculated
from the ages and sampling years of the juvenile and the adult:
$\mathring{A}_\Ad = A_\Ad - (Y_\Ad - B_\Ju)$, but it is valuable
to be able to refer to it explicitly.  The little circle floating above the $A$
in $\mathring{A}_\Ad$ is a notation that we use to mean 
"_at the time of the candidate offspring's birth._"

We use that little circle to denote $\mathring{R}_\Ad$, the candidate mother's reproductive
output at the time of the candidate offspring's birth.  This $\mathring{R}_\Ad$ can
be interpreted as the expected reproductive output of the female adult, and it can
be on a relative scale.  A little bit of explanation is warranted here.  Let's
go back to Mark's fundamental equation for the probability of being a parent-offspring
pair (POP):
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[\mbox{Ad~is~Ju's~mum} &\mid \mbox{stuff~about~Ad~and~Ju}] =  \\
\mathbb{E}\biggl[ &\frac
{\#~\mbox{of~Ad's Ju-like offspring at~}B_\Ju}
{\mbox{Total~\#~of-Ju-like~offspring~at~}B_\Ju}
~\biggl | ~
\mbox{stuff (i.e., covariates) about Ad and Ju}
\biggr ]
\end{aligned}
$$
In words, this is saying that the probability Ad is Ju's mum, given what we know about
Ad and Ju, is calculated as the expected fraction of all the offspring that "are like"
Ju (i.e., that have the same covariates as Ju) at the time of Ju's birth (i.e., at $B_\Ju$)
that were produced by Ad, given what we know about Ad and Ju (i.e., given the covariates
we have observed on Ad and Ju). This is nothing more than the mathematical statement of
what we learned when discussing "Space toast."  

One thing that we did not talk about in our week in Hawaii is that the above expression
is the expected value of a ratio of two variables.  If the numerator and the denominator
were independent random variables, than the expectation of that ratio would be the
ratio of the expectations.  However, Ad's Ju-like offspring are part of the total output
of Ju-like offspring at $B_\Ju$.  Thus, the numerator and the denominator are not
actually independent.  Nonetheless, if the total number of adults is large and the
variance in output of any one adult is not large, the expectation of the ratio above
is well approximate by the ratio of the expectations, so, it is standard in CKMR
to evaluate the kinship probability as:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}[&\mbox{Ad~is~Ju's~mum} \mid \mbox{stuff~about~Ad~and~Ju}] \approx  \\
&\frac
{E[\#~\mbox{of~Ad's Ju-like offspring at~}B_\Ju~|~\mbox{stuff (i.e., covariates) about Ad and Ju}]}
{E[\mbox{Total~\#~of-Ju-like~offspring~at~}B_\Ju~|~\mbox{stuff (i.e., covariates) about Ju and the population]}}
\end{aligned}
$$

In the current case, the covariates are simply age and sampling year, and the
expected reproductive output of a female in the population is the same across
all mature females, which simplifies things considerably.  But, as we go forward
into the more complex cases, it will, perhaps, be valuable to keep in our minds that,
essentially in our CKMR DAG, here, we are treating $\mathring{A}_\Ad$ as the expected value:
$$
\mathring{R}_\Ad \equiv E[\#~\mbox{of~Ad's Ju-like offspring at~}B_\Ju~|~\mbox{stuff (i.e., covariates) about Ad and Ju}],
$$
where "# of offspring" is interpreted as a relative number.
The dependence in that conditional expectation is captured by the arrows in the DAG.
The parents of $\mathring{R}_\Ad$ in the DAG are $B_\Ju$, $\mathring{A}_\Ad$, $Y_\Ad$,
and $A_\mathrm{mat}$, and those are precisely the variables that occur in the
expression for $\mathring{R}_\Ad$, which describes the fact that Ad has reproductive
output typical of any female adult so long as she was mature at $B_\Ju$ and also that
she was not lethally sampled before $B_\Ju$:
$$
\mathring{R}_\Ad = 1\{\mathring{A}_\Ad \geq A_\mathrm{mat}\} 1\{Y_\Ad \geq B_\Ju\}
$$
This is effectively saying that if a female is alive and mature at the time of
the offspring's birth she contributes one unit of expected relative output.
The first indicator requires maturity at
birth. The second requires that lethal capture did not precede that birth.
Sampling in Acme Archipelago is strictly after breeding, so equality $Y_{\mathrm{Ad}}=B_{\mathrm{Ju}}$
is allowed. No forward-survival probability is needed in this example.

$A_{\mathrm{mat}}$ is a supplied knife-edge maturity age. Neither is estimated
by this likelihood.


Every mature female has the same expected output. In those same relative
units, total expected output in the birth year is

$$
h=N_{0,f}\exp\{\lambda(B_{\mathrm{Ju}}-y_0)\},
\qquad \mathring R_{\mathrm{Tot}}=h.
$$

**Unobserved does not mean conditionally random.** Here both reproductive
outputs are determined once their parents in the graph are specified. Their
unshaded nodes retain the biological interpretation and leave room for later
models in which reproduction is genuinely variable.

Finally, $K=1$ means the candidate mother is the offspring's mother; $K=0$
means she is not. It need not mean the two animals are otherwise unrelated.
$K^*$ is the recorded/detected mother-offspring classification.

# The observation model

Write $\alpha$ for the false-positive rate and $\beta$ for the false-negative
rate. They are fixed inputs here, not parameters estimated by the Acme
likelihood. We generally aim to make $\alpha$ negligible and take it as zero.
**Mark's Acme example assumes $\alpha=0$ and $\beta=0$.** Keeping $K$ latent
and $K^*$ observed makes the detection step explicit even in that special case.

\newpage

# Conditional probabilities implied by the graph

Let $\delta_x$ denote a point-mass distribution concentrated at $x$. A
point mass expresses a deterministic conditional relationship; it does not
introduce additional uncertainty. For the six non-root nodes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
B_{\mathrm{Ju}}\mid A_{\mathrm{Ju}},Y_{\mathrm{Ju}}
  &\sim \delta_{Y_{\mathrm{Ju}}-A_{\mathrm{Ju}}},\\[3pt]
\mathring A_{\mathrm{Ad}}\mid A_{\mathrm{Ad}},Y_{\mathrm{Ad}},B_{\mathrm{Ju}}
  &\sim \delta_{A_{\mathrm{Ad}}-Y_{\mathrm{Ad}}+B_{\mathrm{Ju}}},\\[3pt]
\mathring R_{\mathrm{Ad}}\mid\mathring A_{\mathrm{Ad}},Y_{\mathrm{Ad}},B_{\mathrm{Ju}},A_{\mathrm{mat}}
  &\sim \delta_g,\\[3pt]
\mathring R_{\mathrm{Tot}}\mid N_{0,f},\lambda,B_{\mathrm{Ju}},y_0
  &\sim \delta_h,\\[3pt]
K\mid\mathring R_{\mathrm{Ad}},\mathring R_{\mathrm{Tot}}
  &\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}\!\left(
       \frac{\mathring R_{\mathrm{Ad}}}{\mathring R_{\mathrm{Tot}}}\right),\\[3pt]
K^*\mid K,\alpha,\beta
  &\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}\{\alpha+(1-\alpha-\beta)K\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last line means $P(K^*=1\mid K=0)=\alpha$ and
$P(K^*=1\mid K=1)=1-\beta$. Each distribution belongs to a node **conditional
on all its parents**, rather than to an individual arrow.

## Multiply the node conditionals

For compactness, call the first four conditional distributions above
$q_B$, $q_A$, $q_{\mathrm{Ad}}$, and $q_{\mathrm{Tot}}$, respectively, with
their conditioning arguments exactly as displayed. Let $d$ collect their four
node values and $c=(y_0,A_{\mathrm{mat}},\alpha,\beta)$. The conditional joint
law factors as

$$
\begin{split}
p(d,k,k^*\mid z,c,\theta)
={}&q_B\,q_A\,q_{\mathrm{Ad}}\,q_{\mathrm{Tot}}\\
&\times \operatorname{Bern}\!\left(k;
    \frac{\mathring R_{\mathrm{Ad}}}{\mathring R_{\mathrm{Tot}}}\right)
 \operatorname{Bern}\{k^*;\alpha+(1-\alpha-\beta)k\}.
\end{split}
$$

Here $p$ is shorthand for the mixed point-mass/Bernoulli law; $\operatorname{Bern}(k;p)$
is its usual Bernoulli probability mass. The observed and fixed root nodes are
conditioned on. $\theta$ indexes the likelihood; no prior distribution is being
assigned to it.

## Marginalize to the observed pair

The four point masses simply substitute the deterministic values. Summing
over the unobserved $K\in\{0,1\}$ then gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{\mathrm{MOP}}(\theta)&=g/h,\\
p^*(\theta)&=P(K^*=1\mid z,c,\theta)
 =\alpha(1-p_{\mathrm{MOP}})+(1-\beta)p_{\mathrm{MOP}},\\
L_{\mathrm{pair}}(\theta)&=[p^*(\theta)]^{k^*}[1-p^*(\theta)]^{1-k^*}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For Acme's perfect classifications, this reduces to the familiar alive/mature
indicator divided by adult female abundance **in the offspring's birth year**.

\newpage

# A small calculation you can inspect

This function mirrors the named nodes, without environments or special arrays.
It returns intermediates as well as the observed match probability.

```{r}
acme_pair <- function(A_Ju, Y_Ju, A_Ad, Y_Ad, N0_f, lambda,
                      y0, A_mat, alpha = 0, beta = 0) {
  stopifnot(N0_f > 0, alpha >= 0, alpha <= 1,
            beta >= 0, beta <= 1)
  B_Ju <- Y_Ju - A_Ju
  A_Ad_at_birth <- A_Ad - (Y_Ad - B_Ju)
  R_Ad_at_birth <- as.numeric(A_Ad_at_birth >= A_mat &
                               Y_Ad >= B_Ju)
  R_Tot_at_birth <- N0_f * exp(lambda * (B_Ju - y0))
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(R_Tot_at_birth)),
            all(R_Tot_at_birth >= 1))
  p_MOP <- R_Ad_at_birth / R_Tot_at_birth
  p_detected <- alpha * (1 - p_MOP) + (1 - beta) * p_MOP
  data.frame(B_Ju, A_Ad_at_birth, R_Ad_at_birth,
             R_Tot_at_birth, p_MOP, p_detected)
}
```

Two candidate mothers have different ages at the same offspring's birth. The
second was too young to reproduce; the denominator is identical for both.

```{r}
example <- acme_pair(
  A_Ju = 2, Y_Ju = 2015, A_Ad = c(12, 7), Y_Ad = 2016,
  N0_f = 100000, lambda = 0.02, y0 = 2000, A_mat = 8
)
knitr::kable(example, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 7, 7))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
stopifnot(example$A_Ad_at_birth[1] == 9,
          example$A_Ad_at_birth[2] == 4,
          example$p_MOP[1] > 0, example$p_MOP[2] == 0,
          identical(example$p_MOP, example$p_detected))
```

**What can be precomputed?** $B_{\mathrm{Ju}}$, $\mathring A_{\mathrm{Ad}}$,
and $g$ depend only on observed data and supplied constants. The denominator
$h$, the probabilities, and the likelihood contributions must be recomputed
when $\theta$ changes. Parameters and computations depending on them belong
on an AD tape; data-only bookkeeping can be performed beforehand. A pink rim
on $K^*$ concerns its conditional probability, not a changing observed label.

**From one pair to Mark's fit.** Products of pair marginals form a composite
or pseudolikelihood because pairs can share individuals. Mark groups
comparisons into covariate-defined categories and uses a Poisson
pseudolikelihood, with expected detected matches equal to the number of
comparisons times $p^*$. That large-population approximation is a separate
step from the exact single-pair Bernoulli marginal shown here.
